redditSourcedNotes: VERIFY STAGE (5-search budget, all 5 used; no reddit threads were fetched). The research draft was written without web access, so this pass spent its searches on existence/status doubts and on Wikipedia photo titles rather than on reddit sourcing. Confirmed by search: Turks Coffee Bar (1276 Commercial Dr) exists but closes at 6pm daily per Yelp/YellowPages/The Drive BIA, so the draft's 'open late / night hangout' framing was removed; Massy Books (229 E Georgia St) is open and its hidden room is a rare-books room behind a Murphy-door bookcase (Lonely Planet, Broadview, NUVO, Chinatown BIA); Third Beach, Spanish Banks, New Brighton Park and Hinge Park (article also covers Habitat Island) all have matching en.wikipedia.org articles; a 'CRAB Park wikipedia' search returned press/blog pages but no Wikipedia URL, so that title was set to null. Titles NOT search-confirmed and kept only on high prior confidence (flagged in verifyNote): John Hendry Park, Queen Elizabeth Park (Vancouver), Bloedel Conservatory, Nitobe Memorial Garden, Library Square, Dr. Sun Yat-Sen Classical Chinese Garden, Lonsdale Quay. Sources arrays contain only URLs that appeared in this pass's search results; spots with no search were left with empty sources rather than fabricated ones. All 14 spots are real, publicly accessible places; nothing was dropped. Coordinates were sanity-checked against the city centre and neighbourhood geography; Turks Coffee was nudged south to the Charles St corner. Hours for the parks are the City of Vancouver's usual dawn-to-dusk convention and are unverified.

spots.name: Trout Lake (John Hendry Park)
spots.blurb: A small freshwater lake ringed by willows and a gravel loop in the middle of East Van, with a grassy south beach that faces the North Shore mountains. Locals bring a blanket and a book, dogs splash at the off-leash end, and on summer Saturdays the farmers market fills the parking lot. It feels like a neighbourhood backyard rather than a destination.
spots.tips: The lawn on the south shore gets the best evening light on the mountains; the north end near the community centre is quieter. Saturday mornings in market season are busy, weekday evenings are calm.

safety.note: Loop path is only partly lit; busy with joggers and dog walkers until dusk, quiet after.

spots.verifyNote: Not searched (budget); well-known public park. Wikipedia title kept from prior knowledge, not search-confirmed.

spots.name: Spanish Banks Beach
spots.blurb: The long, flat run of beaches west of Jericho where the tide goes out for hundreds of metres and the crowds thin with every block you walk west. You sit on a log with the downtown skyline and the North Shore laid out across the water, and at low tide you can wander far out onto the sand. It is where people go when Kits Beach is too much.
spots.tips: Head to the west end past the last concession for the emptiest logs, and bring a layer because the wind picks up at sunset. Parking is metered in summer and the lots are gated at night, so bike or take the bus if you are staying late.

safety.note: Unlit and very quiet after 10pm. Fine for stargazing with a friend and a headlamp; otherwise leave by dusk.

spots.verifyNote: Wikipedia title confirmed via search (article describes the West Point Grey beaches).

spots.name: Third Beach (Stanley Park)
spots.blurb: The west-facing beach at Ferguson Point on the far side of Stanley Park, a 20-minute walk past the Second Beach crowds and backed by forest instead of apartment towers. Sunsets drop straight into the water, the logs are big enough to lean against, and in past summers a loose drum circle has gathered on Tuesday evenings. It is the beach locals name when asked where they actually watch the sun go down.
spots.tips: Walk or bike the seawall from Second Beach, or park in the Third Beach lot above the concession. There is only one small seasonal concession, so bring what you need, and head back before full dark since the park roads and trails are unlit.

sources.label: Vancouver's Best Places: Third Beach at Stanley Park

safety.note: Stanley Park trails and roads are unlit after dark; return along the seawall with a friend or leave at dusk.

spots.verifyNote: Existence and Wikipedia title confirmed via search.

spots.name: Queen Elizabeth Park summit plaza
spots.blurb: The highest point in the city proper, a former quarry turned into sunken gardens with a wide plaza on top that looks over downtown to the mountains. Locals drive up after dinner to sit on the plaza wall with the city lights below, and early risers get the peaks turning pink before the tour buses arrive. The quarry garden paths below the plaza are where you go for actual quiet.
spots.tips: Park by the Bloedel Conservatory and walk to the plaza's north edge for the classic view; the smaller north quarry garden is far less visited than the big one. Weekend afternoons fill with wedding photos, so aim for early morning or after 8pm.

safety.note: Summit plaza and parking area are lit and used by locals well into the evening; the lower garden paths are not lit.

spots.verifyNote: Not searched (budget); major public park. Wikipedia title kept from prior knowledge, not search-confirmed.

spots.name: Bloedel Conservatory
spots.blurb: A geodesic glass dome on top of Queen Elizabeth Park filled with tropical plants, koi ponds and free-flying birds. On a grey Vancouver afternoon you pay a small admission, sit on a bench in humid warmth while parrots chatter overhead and rain streaks the glass, and lose an hour. It is small enough that it never feels like a museum.
spots.tips: Weekday mornings are near-empty; weekends with kids are louder. Admission is around $10 and the loop is short, so bring a book and settle on a bench rather than lapping it.

safety.note: Staffed indoor space in a lit, busy part of the park.

spots.verifyNote: Not searched (budget); long-running Park Board attraction. Wikipedia title kept from prior knowledge, not search-confirmed; admission price is approximate.

spots.name: Nitobe Memorial Garden
spots.blurb: A walled Japanese stroll garden on the UBC campus, often cited as one of the most authentic outside Japan, with a pond, stone lanterns, a tea house and paths designed to reveal one view at a time. It is quiet in a way few places in the city are; on a drizzly weekday you can have the whole loop to yourself. The small admission fee is exactly why it stays calm.
spots.tips: Rain makes it better, not worse, so go on a wet day with a hood; the bench on the pond's east side gets the best light. Check seasonal hours before heading out because winter days close early and the garden shuts on some off-season weekdays.
spots.hours: Apr-Oct daily ~10am-4:30pm; reduced winter days (check site)

safety.note: Fenced campus garden, open daytime only.

spots.verifyNote: Not searched (budget); established UBC Botanical Garden site. Wikipedia title kept from prior knowledge, not search-confirmed.

spots.name: Vancouver Public Library Central Branch rooftop garden
spots.blurb: The colosseum-shaped central library has a free public rooftop garden on its top floors with terraces looking over downtown toward the North Shore, plus floors of reading rooms below it. On rainy days you pick a window seat on an upper floor and read for hours; when it clears you take the elevator up and sit among the grasses with the city around you. No card, no purchase, no one asking you to move.
spots.tips: The rooftop closes a little before the building and shuts in rough weather, so go up first, then settle inside. The upper floors have the quietest window desks; the atrium cafes on the ground floor are for talking.
spots.hours: Mon-Thu 9:30am-8:30pm; Fri-Sat 9:30am-6pm; Sun 10am-6pm (rooftop may close earlier; check site)

safety.note: Staffed public building in the busy downtown core; surrounding blocks quiet down after closing.

spots.verifyNote: Not searched (budget); the rooftop garden opened to the public in 2018. Wikipedia title 'Library Square' (the Safdie complex containing the Central Branch) kept from prior knowledge, not search-confirmed.

spots.name: Dr. Sun Yat-Sen Park
spots.blurb: The free public half of the Dr. Sun Yat-Sen garden complex in Chinatown: a walled courtyard park with a pond, covered walkways, pavilions and a bridge, sharing a wall with the ticketed classical garden. Locals eat lunch on the benches under the eaves, and the roofed corridors make it one of the few outdoor spots in the city where rain barely matters. It is tiny and easy to miss, which is the point.
spots.tips: Enter from Columbia St or through the Chinese Cultural Centre courtyard off Pender; the covered pavilion on the far side of the pond is the best rain seat. Pair it with the ticketed garden next door if you want the full stroll.
spots.wikipediaTitle: Dr. Sun Yat-Sen Classical Chinese Garden

safety.note: Chinatown borders the Downtown Eastside; the park is calm by day and gates lock at dusk. After dark keep to the lit blocks of Pender and Keefer.

spots.verifyNote: Not searched (budget); the free park adjoins the ticketed garden and is a legitimate Park Board space. Wikipedia title is the article for the whole garden complex (which covers the adjacent public park), kept from prior knowledge, not search-confirmed.

spots.name: CRAB Park at Portside
spots.blurb: A 2.5-hectare waterfront park at the north end of Main St, reached by an overpass over the rail tracks, with a pebble beach, a grassy knoll, a small pier and an unobstructed view of the harbour cranes, cruise ships and the North Shore. It is the closest thing downtown has to a quiet shoreline, and sunrise over the working port is genuinely special. The name stands for Create a Real Available Beach, the residents' committee that fought for it in the 1980s.
spots.tips: Take the Main St overpass from Waterfront Rd and head for the knoll on the west side for the skyline angle, or the pier for the port. Morning and late afternoon are best.

sources.label: Scout Magazine: CRAB Park, a hidden gem on the waterfront

safety.note: On the Downtown Eastside waterfront and has hosted encampments in recent years; friendly and well used by day. Go with a friend and stick to the lit Waterfront Rd approach after dark.

spots.verifyNote: Existence and history confirmed via search (Scout, Vancouver Park Guide, Heritage Foundation). No en.wikipedia.org result surfaced, so wikipediaTitle set to null.

spots.name: Habitat Island & Hinge Park (Olympic Village)
spots.blurb: A tiny constructed island off the Olympic Village seawall, reached by a rocky causeway, where you sit on driftwood with your back to the city and False Creek in front of you. Hinge Park next door is a pocket wetland with a footbridge and a pipe-shaped lookout, and the seawall behind it stays lit and busy late. It is the calmest stretch of a very popular waterfront.
spots.tips: Cross onto the island at lower tide (the causeway can get wet at high water) and take the far point for the skyline. The village plaza with its giant sparrow sculptures is five minutes east if you want a coffee first.

safety.note: Seawall is well lit and busy until late; the island itself has no lights, so move to the plaza benches after dark.

spots.verifyNote: Wikipedia article 'Hinge Park' confirmed via search; it describes both Hinge Park and the connected Habitat Island, so it was used as the photo title.

spots.name: Lonsdale Quay & Burrard Dry Dock Pier
spots.blurb: The North Shore end of the SeaBus, where a long pier at the old Burrard Dry Dock juts into the inlet facing the whole downtown skyline. You sit on the pier's benches or the steps at the Shipyards and watch the lights come on across the water; in winter there is a covered plaza and a skating rink, in summer a night market. It is busy in a relaxed way and never really dark.
spots.tips: Ride the SeaBus over after work for the golden-hour crossing and sit at the end of the pier; the Quay Market food hall is a warm fallback when it rains. Summer Friday night-market crowds thin by 10pm.

safety.note: Lit, busy waterfront with SeaBus service until after midnight.

spots.verifyNote: Not searched (budget); well-known transit hub and public pier. Wikipedia title kept from prior knowledge, not search-confirmed.

spots.name: Turks Coffee Bar (Commercial Drive)
spots.blurb: A scuffed-up neighbourhood cafe that has anchored Commercial Drive since the 1990s, billed as the Drive's first indie coffee bar, with worn wooden seating, solid espresso and a house habit of leaving you alone. It works as a rainy-afternoon reading spot or a place to nurse a coffee while the Drive's foot traffic rolls past the window. Nobody rushes you.
spots.tips: Grab a window seat for people-watching or the back tables if you want to work; it is loudest on weekend afternoons. It closes at 6pm, so it is a daytime spot. Grandview Park is right across the Drive when the rain lets up.

sources.label: The Drive BIA: Turks Coffee Bar
Yelp: Turk's Coffee Bar, 1276 Commercial Dr

safety.note: Busy, well-lit stretch of Commercial Drive; the cafe closes at 6pm.

spots.verifyNote: Confirmed open at 1276 Commercial Dr via search; listed hours are 7am-6pm daily, so the draft's 'open late / night' claims, vibes and best times were removed. Coordinates nudged to the Charles St corner.

spots.name: Massy Books
spots.blurb: An Indigenous-owned new-and-used bookshop on East Georgia St with tall shelves, a strong Indigenous and BC section, and a hidden rare-books room behind a folding bookcase door. It is the kind of shop where you can browse an armful of books for a long time and nobody minds, and the back room is close to silent even when the front is busy. A rainy-afternoon Vancouver classic.
spots.tips: Ask staff about the hidden room if you cannot find the bookcase door, and go weekday afternoons for the emptiest aisles. The Chinatown bakeries on Keefer are a block away for a cheap snack.

sources.label: Broadview: Massy Books is more than a business
NUVO: A look inside Massy Books
Vancouver Chinatown BIA directory: Massy Books

safety.note: Staffed shop on a busy Chinatown block; the area quiets after dark.

spots.verifyNote: Confirmed open at 229 E Georgia St via search; hidden room is a rare-books room behind a Murphy-door bookcase, blurb adjusted accordingly. Hours unverified.

spots.name: New Brighton Park
spots.blurb: Vancouver's oldest park, a wedge of lawn and shoreline between the PNE grounds and the port terminals, facing the Second Narrows bridge, the grain elevators and the North Shore peaks. There is a heated outdoor pool in summer, a restored salt marsh, and long stretches of grass where dog walkers and East Van locals sit and watch container ships slide under the bridge. Few people from outside the neighbourhood know it exists.
spots.tips: Enter from the McGill St overpass at Windermere; the benches on the east point look straight up the inlet and catch the morning light. Bring a coffee from the Drive because the park has none.

safety.note: Public park reached by a road overpass over the rail line; well used by dog walkers and swimmers in daylight, dim after dark.

spots.verifyNote: Wikipedia title confirmed via search (article describes the Hastings-Sunrise waterfront park, pool and off-leash area).
